ruled_out.why: The failing spans come from one pod, ts-travel-service-cbf9bf77c-6rnnm, and the handler keeps logging and completing requests through the window. The k8s.container.restarts and k8s.pod.uptime metrics do not exist for ts-travel-service in either period, so there is no restart signal to show a pod went down and came back.
The same pod keeps emitting logs and spans throughout the abnormal window, so it is not silent or gone.

The requests arrive and the handler runs (INFO logs inside getRouteByTripId), so the connection from both callers is up. Failures are fast 500 responses, not hangs until timeout. The survey's hubble drop counts for the travel connections are 0.
Loss would show as retransmits or timeouts with long tails. The failing server spans are uniformly about 4 ms and return a response with status 500, not a timeout.
Delay would lengthen the Client-to-Server gap. Here the caller spans are 3 to 7 ms and the server self-time is about 4 ms, so nothing is added on the wire.
No deserialization or checksum errors appear in the logs. The error is a Spring dispatcher exception after the handler starts.
Nothing in the telemetry points to duplicated packets, and the failures are consistent errors rather than repeats.
Responses are small and fail at once, so bandwidth limits would not produce a uniform 500 in 4 ms.
An aborted exchange would show a cut connection or an application-level transport error. Here the server span carries a complete 500 response and the exception is logged inside the process.

The status is 500 together with a server-side exception on the same route, so the 500 is the consequence of the throw, not a rewritten status on a healthy response. The handler does not complete normally and only the code changes.
Failing requests are fast (about 4 ms), not slowed at the HTTP layer.
The request is well formed (INFO logs show valid tripIds G1234, G1235, G1236, D1345 for all 2528 calls), and the response is a failure status, not a parsed-but-wrong body.

The failing getRouteByTripId spans have no children at all, and the normal period's TripRepository.findByTripId child (325 calls, 1.68 ms) is absent from the failing spans. The DB call is never reached, so a SQL-layer throw is not the source.
Nothing reaches the database on the failing route, so there is no slow DB call to measure.
The method does not slow down; its self-time drops from 16.4 ms in the normal period to 3.9 ms, and it ends in an exception.
No DNS or name-resolution text appears in the SEVERE or INFO logs for this service, and no connection to a wrong name is attempted.
The handler reaches its own code and throws; nothing indicates a connection to an unintended peer.
Nothing in the telemetry suggests timestamp reordering; the failure is a per-request exception with a steady 4 ms duration.

A CPU-saturated process would slow requests, not make them fail uniformly at once. The mean latency of the route falls from 16 ms to 4 ms in the failing period. Container CPU time shows values of 589 to 762 in the abnormal period, but I did not compare them against the normal period.
Same as process_cpu_saturated: saturation slows work rather than producing immediate 500 responses. The container CPU series was not compared to normal, so this is only weakly excluded.
Memory pressure would show as OOM, swap or cgroup events, and none appear in the logs; I did not check memory series against normal.
No OutOfMemoryError or heap-exhaustion text appears; the thrown error is IllegalArgumentException, not an in-process OOM.
GC pauses would stall all requests on the pod, not produce uniform exceptions on one route. Other travel routes on the same pod (POST /trips/left) do not error.
The fault is a thrown exception that escapes to the dispatcher, not a value returned from a method. The method's return path is never reached.
